questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose Australia because it was far away and completely different from everything in Denmark. I also chose it, because everyone speaks english, so it would be easier to talk with everyone.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was easy. The university sent me a folder with everything I needed to know before I got to Australia and they also gave me a free shuttle bus ride to the on-campus dormitory I stayed in. I had some issues with choosing my courses, but i got quick help from both the University of Copenhagen and Western Sydney University.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: A free shuttle bus ride and an orientation event about the university.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I think they tried to help as much as they could, but a lot of the exchange students (myself included) were a bit confused in the beginning about how everything worked. For example with the study website and the social events,

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The university has several campus villages in different parts of (outer) Sydney. Compared to everything else they were relatively affordable, but not cheap at all. However, as far as i now, the village in Parramatta is the most lively one and the closest to the city itself.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer:
The university itself had free breakfast on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, which is about 5 minutes away from the village. No other meal plans are available. 
Every apartment in the village has a kitchen.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
You meet a lot of really nice people in the campus housing who are doing the same exchange stay as you are. However, it should be noted, that the village is far away from Sydney CBD. It takes about 15 minutes with the free university shuttle bus or regular bus (OR 30 minutes walking) to Parramatta train station, and then 45 minutes by train to Sydney CBD. A lot of the time, I travelled with other people from the village, and we used the travel time to get to know each other really well. 

It should also be noted, that you cannot choose your roommates. Some of my friends got really lucky and had some great ones, but I did not and preferred not to use the common room in the apartment. The university housing has a lot of different people, and you will both meet weird people and some extremely nice people that will make the exchange stay a lot better.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was confusing. I got a lot of help from my friend who went to the same university as me. I also sent a lot of emails to the university itself, who were good at helping me.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I cannot remember the full details. But in order to get some of the courses approved you need to submit a special form to them (for example with post-graduate classes, where you just need to say that you are post graduate, and you can get it)

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: email and the service hub in the univeristy

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: semi-successful. I ended up getting 2 courses I wanted, and 2 courses I had to get because I had no other options at the moment. Some of the courses could not be approved by my home university and some did not get approved by my host university.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Look at all the courses that are available and submit the course approval form to the university of Copenhagen as quickly as you can. They will require a learning guide to approve it. The best way to get this is to wait until you get your host university email and then you can contact every professor you need to learning guide from, and they will respond quicker than from other foreign emails. It will still take some weeks if you are unlucky.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was almost embarrassed by how easy the academic courses were. I did not struggle at all and passed them easily. I felt like I would have been challenged more if I stayed at the University of Copenhagen. Everyone I met from Europe felt the same way about how easy it was to pass.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The levels went from 1 to 7 as far as I remember. My level 7 course did not feel difficult at all.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: They liked small classes. I did not see any lecture halls with room for a lot of people, and most of my courses was about 20 people. The final grade is not based on one exam but on assignments, presentations and exams.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
BLDG7006 Financing Cities in the Global Economy
COMP2023 Mathematical Programming
COMP7024 Programming for Data Science
ECON3014 International Finance

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
COMP2023 Mathematical Programming: If you are interested in Python programming. The professor was a bit confused sometimes, but he got the spirit. 
COMP7024 Programming for Data Science: If you are interested in R programming. The professor was super nice and really nerdy about R, but you could really feel the passion he had about it.

The other two I would NOT recommend.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I had to rebook flights and had to add extra luggage going home.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Flights

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: They did not have a lot of interesting things.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Sports groups, gaming groups, specific country groups.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
The only good one was the "out and about" group, but you need to book those activities FAST.
I also went to a free self-defense class on campus which was fun.
and the free food events.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Do the east coast trip at the end after exams. 
Explore Sydney: Go to Manly, Watsons Bay and the Blue Mountains. Visit all the markets in Glebe, Manly etc. 
Australia and Sydney has a LOT to offer.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was OK. However, we mostly just talked with our exchange group friends, and I rarely had long conversations with true Australian people.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: They are friendly, but most of them are not interested in having friends that they will only see for half a year.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: They are pretty European. However, they do swear a lot, and will swear at you if you annoy them.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: It's difficult to say because Australia has so many different cultures and people. You dont go to Sydney and find a lot of "typical aussie" restaurants, but you will find food and stuff from all over the world.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Everything is expensive
Travel and explore even though it is expensive 
Dont worry too much about being able to pass the courses

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting some of the greatest people that i could spend a lot of time with and travel around Australia with.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Learning to be on my own. I chose to travel alone a bit, and learned that I did not have to depend on other people to want the same as me in order for me to do it. I really appreciated both being on my own, and being with my friends.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: No

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
